subject: Accounting
title: The Balanced Scorecard
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Balanced Scorecard usable.

hook.text: Profit alone doesn't tell the full story. A balanced scorecard looks at four dimensions.

buildup.text: It measures financial results, customer satisfaction, internal processes, and learning and growth.

discovery.text: A company might be profitable today but failing at innovation—threatening its future.

twist.text: Kaplan and Norton created the balanced scorecard in 1992. It's still one of the most used strategy tools.

climax.text: The framework forces managers to think beyond short-term profits and invest in long-term health.

punchline.text: Four perspectives. One complete picture of performance.

quiz.question: How many perspectives does the balanced scorecard use?

details.summary: The balanced scorecard measures organizational performance across four perspectives: financial, customer, internal processes, and learning and growth. This topic explains how it connects strategy to measurable objectives and prevents overreliance on financial metrics alone.
details.whyItMatters: Financial results are lagging indicators—they tell you what already happened. The balanced scorecard adds leading indicators from customers, processes, and learning that predict future performance.
takeaways: The four perspectives are financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth
Strategy maps link objectives across perspectives to show cause-and-effect relationships
A well-balanced scorecard limits each perspective to four to seven key measures

faq.question: What is the balanced scorecard?
faq.answer: The balanced scorecard is a strategic performance framework developed by Kaplan and Norton that measures an organization across four perspectives: financial performance, customer satisfaction, internal process efficiency, and organizational learning and growth.

faq.question: Why is the balanced scorecard better than using financial metrics alone?
faq.answer: Financial metrics only show past results. The balanced scorecard adds leading indicators—customer satisfaction predicts future revenue, process efficiency predicts cost trends, and learning metrics predict innovation capacity. It gives a complete performance picture.
